title: All in His creation
hookLine: the good and the lost are all within His play

cards: Yesterday's list was easy to love. Pilgrims. Poets.
Meditators. If the stanza had stopped there, it would be a nice hymn about good people. It doesn't stop there.
The second stanza keeps the same drumbeat, kaee kot, many millions, and turns it on everyone we'd rather leave out of the picture. The proud. The cruel.
The thieves. The gossips. The ones chasing money until they drop.

teach.h: THE PROUD, THE CRUEL, THE THIEVES.
teach.b: The second stanza goes: many millions are proud. Many millions are blind and ignorant. Many millions are misers, hard of heart.
Many millions are cold inside, without feeling. Many millions steal what belongs to others. Many millions slander others.
Many millions toil for wealth. Many millions wander in foreign lands.
Then the turn, addressed straight to God: whatever You attach them to, to that they are attached.
And the last line: Nanak, only the Creator knows His own creation. No verdict. Nobody's sentenced.
These too are in the creation, and the One who made it is the only one who truly knows it. That doesn't mean Sikh teaching shrugs at cruelty or theft.
The Gurus spoke hard words against oppression and greed, and Sikhs are asked to stand up for those who are wronged.
But this stanza is about something else: the urge to stand outside the creation and sort it into the saved and the lost, as if we had made it. Kartaa is the word for the Creator, the Doer.
Only the Kartaa knows the creation; all of it is within His play.
That's humbling, and oddly freeing: you don't have to be everybody's judge. And this is where the week ends. Seven days ago, the true aparas.
Then pandit, nihkaram, Singh and Kaur and the badge set down.
Then the crowd: so many, many millions, and today, all of them, in the play.

how: Sikhs read this stanza of Sukhmani Sahib as a reminder that only the Creator knows the creation, while still standing against injustice as the Gurus taught.

o: the Creator, the Doer of all
the part each person must play
a judge who sorts the saved

games.q: all in His creation — tap the pairs.

s: the second stanza ends by sentencing the proud and cruel
no verdict: only the Creator knows His own creation.
the stanza lists thieves and slanderers among the many millions
the same drumbeat, kaee kot, turned on everyone.
not judging means Sikhs shrug at injustice
the Gurus spoke hard words against oppression; this stanza is about not playing the Creator.

games.q: the stanza has listed the proud, the cruel and the thieves. what comes next?
o: Nanak, only the Creator knows His creation.
a call to drive them out.
games.why: whatever You attach them to, to that they are attached; only the Kartaa knows the creation.

practice: Bring to mind someone you've been judging lately, a relative, a coworker, a stranger online, and without arguing with your judgment or pretending they're right, picture them inside the same creation as you, held by the same hands.
Breathe in: they're in the play; breathe out: so am I. You can still disagree and still say no; you're only setting down the gavel for a while.

wordCard.voice: Kartaa, the Creator, the Doer. The proud and the lost, the cruel and the kind, many millions, all within His play; only the Kartaa knows it.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: kartaa, the Creator, the Doer; ashtpadi ten says only the Kartaa knows the creation.

carryVoice: Your line: all in the play. Only the Kartaa knows the whole of it. Another week, done.

sources.work: Guru Granth Sahib (Guru Arjan, Gauri Sukhmani)
